## Presence can be scored in three ways

[Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd) scored its calls
of present or absent by accuracy, and
[Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd#three-measures-count-misses-and-false-alarms-apart)
added sensitivity, specificity and precision. All four count the calls at one threshold.
But a model that predicts presence gives every station a probability, which also ranks
the stations from most to least likely to hold the species. So there are three things to
score: the calls, the ranking and the probabilities themselves. This page adds the
measures most used in machine learning for each, and shows that a model can look good on
one and poor on another.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## Measures at one threshold count the calls

Three summaries of the calls are common in machine learning. Each turns the four counts
at a threshold into one number: true presences, false alarms, misses and true absences,
often set out as a two-by-two table called the **confusion matrix**.

| Measure | What it is | A rule that calls every station present scores |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accuracy | the share of calls that are right | the share of stations with the species |
| **F1** | an average of precision and sensitivity, pulled towards the lower of the two | close to 1 when presence is common |
| **Balanced accuracy** | the average of sensitivity and specificity | 0.5 |
| **MCC**, the Matthews correlation coefficient | the correlation between the calls and the truth, from −1 to 1 | nothing: its calls never vary, so there is no correlation to work out |

F1 is built from precision and sensitivity, and neither counts the **true absences**, the
absent stations called absent. F1 suits a search for something rare, where the absences
are many and uninteresting. Balanced accuracy and MCC count every cell, and treat
presence and absence alike.

## ROC AUC scores the ranking at every threshold

[Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd#upsampling-gives-the-same-answers-as-a-lower-threshold)
drew a model's sensitivity against its specificity at every threshold. That curve is the
**ROC curve** (receiver operating characteristic, a name from radar). The area under it,
the **ROC AUC**, sums up the whole curve in one number, so models can be compared before
a threshold is chosen. It is also the share of pairs, one station with the species and
one without, in which the station with the species gets the higher probability. A ROC
AUC of 1 ranks every station with the species above every station without it; 0.5 is no
better than ranking at random.

ROC AUC depends only on the order of the probabilities. Raising every probability, or
squeezing them all towards 0.5, leaves the order and the ROC AUC unchanged.

## Log loss scores the probabilities themselves

Log loss, from
[Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd#counts-and-presence-have-their-own-losses),
charges each station for the probability the model gave to what happened: little for a
high probability of presence where the species was found, a lot for a confident call that
turned out wrong. Lower is better. It rewards probabilities that are spread out, high
where the species is and low where it is not, and **calibrated**: of the stations given
0.8, about 8 in 10 hold the species. ROC AUC sees only the first of these.

::: {.diagram}
![ROC AUC and log loss on two sets of eight probabilities. Left, every station with the species is ranked above every station without it, but all eight probabilities are high: ROC AUC is perfect, and log loss charges heavily for the absent stations called likely. Right, one pair is in the wrong order, but the probabilities sit near the truth: ROC AUC is a little lower and log loss much lower. The two measures rank the two sets in opposite orders.](img/auc-and-log-loss.svg){fig-alt="Two cards, each with four stations where the species is present, drawn filled, and four where it is absent, drawn open, placed along an axis of predicted probability of presence from 0 to 1. Left, right order, too sure of presence: the present stations sit at 0.85 and above, the absent ones between 0.6 and 0.8; ROC AUC 1.00, log loss 0.66. Right, some order wrong, honest: the present stations sit between 0.4 and 0.9 and the absent ones between 0.1 and 0.6, so one absent station is ranked above one present station; ROC AUC 0.94, log loss 0.40. A note says ROC AUC is the share of present–absent pairs in which the present station has the higher probability, and log loss charges each station for the probability it gave to what happened, most for a confident miss."}
:::

## Worked example

The outcome is `present`, whether the species was caught at a station at all. Three
models predict it:

- **Predicting the share present**: every station gets the share of the fitted stations
  with the species. It has no skill, and the other two should beat it.
- **Logistic regression**, from
  [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd), with each
  input entered as a straight line in the log-odds.
- **Random forest**, from
  [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd). For presence,
  each tree gives the share of stations with the species in the leaf a station falls in,
  and the forest averages those shares into a probability.

As on [Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd), every model is
cross-validated on the same ten folds of sites, and each measure is worked out from the
pooled out-of-fold probabilities.

### Preparing the data

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

set.seed(61)
folds <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 10)

inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu",
            "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude")

presence_recipe <- recipe(reformulate(inputs, "present"), data = survey) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

forest <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |>
  set_mode("classification")

models <- list(
  "Predicting the share present" = null_model(mode = "classification"),
  "Logistic regression"          = logistic_reg(),
  "Random forest"                = forest
)

# every station's out-of-fold probability of presence, in the survey's order
out_of_fold <- map(models, \(model) {
  fit_resamples(workflow(presence_recipe, model), folds,
                metrics = metric_set(roc_auc),
                control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |>
    collect_predictions() |>
    arrange(.row) |>
    pull(.pred_yes)
})

predictions <- as_tibble(out_of_fold) |>
  mutate(present = survey$present) |>
  pivot_longer(-present, names_to = "model", values_to = "probability") |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model))

tibble(stations = nrow(survey),
       `share present` = mean(survey$present == "yes"),
       `outcome levels` = str_flatten(levels(survey$present), ", "))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, balanced_accuracy_score, f1_score,
                             log_loss, matthews_corrcoef, roc_auc_score, roc_curve)
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()
present = (survey["present"] == "yes").to_numpy()

folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=61)

inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu",
          "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"]
categorical = ["substrate", "season"]
numeric = [c for c in inputs if c not in categorical]

def with_inputs(model):
    recipe = ColumnTransformer([
        # scaling leaves an unpenalised fit unchanged and helps the solver
        ("numeric", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                              ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric),
        ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical),
    ])
    return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)])

models = {
    "Predicting the share present": DummyClassifier(strategy="prior"),
    "Logistic regression": LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=5000),
    # as ranger does for probabilities: a few inputs at each question,
    # and no split of a leaf with fewer than 10 stations
    "Random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt",
                                            min_samples_split=10, random_state=1),
}

# every station's out-of-fold probability of presence, in the survey's order;
# column 1 of predict_proba is the probability of True
out_of_fold = {name: cross_val_predict(with_inputs(model), survey[inputs], present,
                                       cv=folds, groups=survey["site_id"],
                                       method="predict_proba")[:, 1]
               for name, model in models.items()}

predictions = (pd.DataFrame(out_of_fold).assign(present=present)
               .melt(id_vars="present", var_name="model", value_name="probability"))

pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "share present": [present.mean()]})
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: helpers
#| include: false
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
pct <- function(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1)
share_present <- mean(survey$present == "yes")
n_absent <- sum(survey$present == "no")
```

The species was caught at `r pct(share_present)` of the `r nrow(survey)` stations, so
presence is the common answer here. yardstick treats the first level of the outcome as
the event a measure is about, and `present` lists `yes` first, so every measure below is
about presence. In scikit-learn the outcome is `True` for presence, which its measures
take as the event by default.

### F1 cannot tell the models from calling every station present

At the default threshold of 0.5, predicting the share present calls every station
present, since it gives every station a probability near `r f2(share_present)`.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: calls
calls <- predictions |>
  mutate(called = factor(if_else(probability >= 0.5, "yes", "no"),
                         levels = c("yes", "no")))

at_threshold <- calls |>
  summarise(`true absences` = sum(called == "no" & present == "no"),
            accuracy = accuracy_vec(present, called),
            F1 = f_meas_vec(present, called),
            `balanced accuracy` = bal_accuracy_vec(present, called),
            # NA where the calls never vary
            MCC = suppressWarnings(mcc_vec(present, called)),
            .by = model)

at_threshold |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Python

```{python}
def at_threshold(g, threshold=0.5):
    called = g.probability >= threshold
    return pd.Series({
        "true absences": int((~called & ~g.present).sum()),
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(g.present, called),
        "F1": f1_score(g.present, called),
        "balanced accuracy": balanced_accuracy_score(g.present, called),
        # scikit-learn gives 0 where the calls never vary
        "MCC": matthews_corrcoef(g.present, called),
    })

calls = (predictions.groupby("model", sort=False)
         .apply(at_threshold, include_groups=False).reset_index())

calls.round(3)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: call-numbers
#| include: false
call_of <- function(name, measure) at_threshold[[measure]][at_threshold$model == name]
rule <- "Predicting the share present"
f1_gap <- max(abs(at_threshold$F1 - call_of(rule, "F1")))
```

Accuracy and F1 barely move. The rule that calls every station present has an F1 of
`r f3(call_of(rule, "F1"))`, and neither model is more than `r f3(f1_gap)` away from it.
The models differ in the true absences: of the `r n_absent` stations without the species,
logistic regression called `r call_of("Logistic regression", "true absences")` absent and
the random forest `r call_of("Random forest", "true absences")`. F1 never counts those
stations, so it cannot see the difference.

Balanced accuracy and MCC can. Balanced accuracy puts the rule at
`r f3(call_of(rule, "balanced accuracy"))`, logistic regression at
`r f3(call_of("Logistic regression", "balanced accuracy"))` and the forest at
`r f3(call_of("Random forest", "balanced accuracy"))`, and MCC gives
`r f3(call_of("Logistic regression", "MCC"))` and
`r f3(call_of("Random forest", "MCC"))`. MCC cannot be worked out for the rule:
yardstick reports it as missing, and scikit-learn as 0, the value for calls unrelated to
the truth. Both models are only a little better than the rule at this threshold, and the
forest is the better of the two.

### The forest ranks the stations better

Predicting the share present is left out here. Within a fold it gives every station the
same probability, so it ranks nothing.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: roc
ranked <- filter(predictions, model != rule) |>
  mutate(model = fct_drop(model))

ranked |>
  summarise(`ROC AUC` = round(roc_auc_vec(present, probability), 3), .by = model)
```

## Python

```{python}
ranked = predictions[predictions["model"] != "Predicting the share present"]

(ranked.groupby("model", sort=False)
 .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({"ROC AUC": roc_auc_score(g.present, g.probability)}),
        include_groups=False)
 .reset_index().round(3))
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: roc-numbers
#| include: false
aucs <- ranked |>
  summarise(auc = roc_auc_vec(present, probability), .by = model)
auc_of <- function(name) aucs$auc[aucs$model == name]
curves <- ranked |>
  group_by(model) |>
  roc_curve(present, probability) |>
  ungroup()
# the calls at 0.5 from the first part, as points on each curve
default_calls <- calls |>
  filter(model != rule) |>
  summarise(sensitivity = sensitivity_vec(present, called),
            specificity = specificity_vec(present, called), .by = model)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-roc
#| fig-cap: !expr glue::glue("ROC curves of the two models' out-of-fold probabilities, showing sensitivity against specificity at every threshold. The dashed diagonal is ranking at random. The points mark the default threshold of 0.5, high on sensitivity and low on specificity. The forest's curve, with a ROC AUC of {f3(auc_of('Random forest'))}, lies above logistic regression's, at {f3(auc_of('Logistic regression'))}.")
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("A plot of sensitivity from 0 to 1 against specificity running from 1 on the left to 0 on the right, with a dashed diagonal from the bottom left to the top right. Two curves rise from the bottom left corner to the top right corner, both above the diagonal. The orange curve, the random forest, lies above the blue one, logistic regression, along most of its length. A point on each curve marks the threshold of 0.5, both near the top right corner, logistic regression at specificity {f2(default_calls$specificity[default_calls$model == 'Logistic regression'])} and the forest at {f2(default_calls$specificity[default_calls$model == 'Random forest'])}.")
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(curves, aes(specificity, sensitivity, colour = model)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 1, slope = 1, colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_path(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = default_calls, size = 3.2) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_colour_ml() +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Specificity", y = "Sensitivity", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::

The forest's ROC AUC is `r f3(auc_of("Random forest"))`, and logistic regression's
`r f3(auc_of("Logistic regression"))`: in about `r round(100 * auc_of("Random forest"))`
of 100 pairs of a station with the species and one without, the forest gives the station
with the species the higher probability. Its curve lies above the other along most of its
length, so whatever threshold is chosen, the forest can reach the same sensitivity with
fewer false alarms. The points show why the first part made the two models look so alike:
0.5 sits near the top right corner, where the curves are closest.

### Log loss rewards probabilities that are spread out and calibrated

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: log-loss
probability_scores <- predictions |>
  summarise(`log loss` = mn_log_loss_vec(present, probability),
            lowest = min(probability), highest = max(probability),
            .by = model)

probability_scores |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Python

```{python}
probability_scores = (predictions.groupby("model", sort=False)
                      .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({
                          "log loss": log_loss(g.present, g.probability),
                          "lowest": g.probability.min(),
                          "highest": g.probability.max(),
                      }), include_groups=False)
                      .reset_index())

probability_scores.round(3)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: log-loss-numbers
#| include: false
loss_of <- function(name) probability_scores$`log loss`[probability_scores$model == name]
spread_of <- function(name, end) probability_scores[[end]][probability_scores$model == name]
# eight groups of equal size by predicted probability, for the calibration plot
calibration <- ranked |>
  mutate(group = ntile(probability, 8), .by = model) |>
  summarise(predicted = mean(probability), observed = mean(present == "yes"),
            .by = c(model, group))
range_of <- function(name) range(calibration$predicted[calibration$model == name])
```

A **calibration plot** checks the second half of what log loss rewards. It sorts each
model's stations by their predicted probability into eight groups of
`r nrow(survey) / 8`, and plots each group's average probability against the share of
its stations where the species was caught.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-calibration
#| fig-cap: !expr glue::glue("Calibration of the two models' out-of-fold probabilities, in eight groups of {nrow(survey) / 8} stations each. Points on the dashed diagonal mean the probabilities can be read as chances. The grey cross is predicting the share present, which gives every station the same probability. Both models stay close to the diagonal; the forest's groups spread from {f2(range_of('Random forest')[1])} to {f2(range_of('Random forest')[2])}, wider than logistic regression's.")
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("A plot of the share of stations with the species against the average predicted probability, both from 0.3 to 1, with a dashed diagonal. Eight blue points for logistic regression run from {f2(range_of('Logistic regression')[1])} to {f2(range_of('Logistic regression')[2])} along the diagonal, a little above or below it. Eight orange points for the random forest run further, from {f2(range_of('Random forest')[1])} to {f2(range_of('Random forest')[2])}, also close to the diagonal. A single grey cross for predicting the share present sits on the diagonal at {f2(share_present)}.")
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(calibration, aes(predicted, observed, colour = model)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  annotate("point", x = share_present, y = share_present, shape = 4, size = 5,
           stroke = 1.6, colour = "grey45") +
  scale_colour_ml() +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0.3, 1), ylim = c(0.3, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Average predicted probability", y = "Share with the species",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::

Both models' groups stay close to the diagonal, so their probabilities can be read as
chances. Predicting the share present is calibrated too: it says
`r f2(share_present)` everywhere, and the species was caught at `r pct(share_present)`
of the stations. What it lacks is spread, and log loss charges it the most, at
`r f3(loss_of(rule))`. Logistic regression lowers that to
`r f3(loss_of("Logistic regression"))` and the forest to
`r f3(loss_of("Random forest"))`, `r pct(1 - loss_of("Random forest") / loss_of(rule))`
below the rule. The forest gains by spreading its probabilities further, from
`r f2(spread_of("Random forest", "lowest"))` to `r f2(spread_of("Random forest", "highest"))`
against logistic regression's `r f2(spread_of("Logistic regression", "lowest"))` to
`r f2(spread_of("Logistic regression", "highest"))`, while staying calibrated. The spread
that lowers its log loss is the same that gave it the higher ROC AUC.
Here the three kinds of measure agree on the order of the models. The diagram above shows
that they need not, so the measure to report follows from how the predictions will be
used, which [Choosing measures that match the objective](choosing-a-metric.qmd) sets
out.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- Presence can be scored on the **calls** at one threshold, on the **ranking** the
  probabilities make, or on the **probabilities** themselves. A model can do well on one
  and poorly on another.
- **F1** never counts the true absences. With the species at `r pct(share_present)` of
  stations, calling every station present scored an F1 of `r f3(call_of(rule, "F1"))`,
  within `r f3(f1_gap)` of both models. **Balanced accuracy** and **MCC** count every
  cell and told the models apart.
- **ROC AUC** is the area under the curve of sensitivity against specificity: the share
  of pairs, one station with the species and one without, ranked the right way round.
  It is 0.5 for ranking at random, and it ignores how high or low the probabilities are.
- **Log loss** rewards probabilities that are both spread out and **calibrated**. A
  calibration plot shows whether a predicted 0.8 means 8 in 10.
- yardstick treats the first level of the outcome as the event. Check the levels before
  trusting any of these measures.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Add a fourth model: logistic regression with `step_upsample(present)` from the
   `themis` package at the end of its recipe, as in
   [Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd). Predict first:
   does its ROC AUC or its log loss move more?
2. Score the three models on `rare_species` instead of `present`. How does the F1 of
   predicting the share present change when the species is rare?
